

# Developer Productivity: The 

My previous article, *Maximizing Developer Effectiveness*, focused on speeding up feedback loops and reducing friction. This companion piece focuses on the other side of developer productivity: how effective developers build better products that are more valuable to their customers

## Developers make value by innovating

A productive developer creates value by innovating. Sometimes that's thinking up radical new ideas, sometimes incremental product improvements. They evolve applications for better efficiency or reliability, build scrappy prototypes, and put due diligence into hard technical decisions. They can prioritize what to do and when because they can estimate impact to the customer and business. Empowered to be innovative on behalf of the customer and the business, they make informed decisions from deep knowledge of customer motivations and problems. They draw on the expertise of domain specialists and researchers. They move fast because risk is low and they have an effective developer environment. An engineering platform gives them a safety net to experiment and measure impact quickly. Failure is treated as learning, not cause for blame.

This enviroment is hard to get right. In a small company it may happen organically through necessity, there aren’t layers of indirection yet, colleagues are  transparent and there is narturally less risk.. But as a company scales, complexity, bureaucracy and protectionism creep in. Developers tasks are dictated by a rigid project plan or what will please their manager. The feedback cycle from idea to a customer getting value has become so long, it’s hard to decipher what is or isn’t making an impact. 

## The factory antipattern

This is the premise I thought about when, started writing this article over 3 years ago, At the time where there was a focus on developer productivity. We were coming out of the pandemic, when companies realized debt is no longer cheap and they can’t hire their way out of [problems](http://problems.It). Companies were looking for ways to identify developer productivity. It struck me that a lot of developer productivity frameworks were using an outdated view of software development – treating it like a factory line. In this model, we reduce the worth of a developer to write code to fulfill predetermined requirements; a coding robot to churn out new pages and widgets. It is appealing to think of software develop in this way, it makes it easy to quantify, we can just measure how fast developers are completing their assigned tasks. 

There are parts of development that are “factory like”; repetitive, low value tasks that should be standardized, and completed to an exacting quality every time. However the difficult part of software product development, designing and building something new and novel that delights customers, is not standardized, and this is where effective developers spend their energy. When I think about productivity and why we hire developers, I don’t believe it’s just for their ability to code quickly, it’s their judgement, their ideas, their ability to design and scale software, in my mind I couldn’t separate the innovation part from “developer producitivty” no matter how much easier it makes the equation.. 

Metrics like developer velocity, pull request rate, and number of merges, are popular measurements of developer productivity. These metrics provide signal to derive insights on efficiency, but they solely reflect a part of the developer lifecycle and tell you little about quality, outcome and invention of what is being produced. When we overemphasize these metrics, and don’t take into account other signals, we can inadvertently incentivize the wrong outcome – a lot of code and software that doesn’t create value for customers. 

Thus, when we think about optimizing productivity, we should foster a culture that prioritizes a product-centric approach; that fully utilizes developers’ creative and cognitive skills. Marty Cagan in his seminal product management book [“Inspired”](https://www.svpg.com/books/inspired-how-to-create-tech-products-customers-love-2nd-edition/), states  “"If you're just using your engineers to code, you're only getting about half their value'”. \<Studio model\> 

Since I thought about this premisze, the software developement world has been unended with AI. With AI now promising to make teams more efficient. Code generation is cheaper and AI Native teams are transforming many process through AI (writing, operations, knowledge access). We continually hear that developers have time for “high value” or “highly differentiating" work. Creating an environment where a developers are empowered to be innovation, with feedback loops directly from the custoerm is even more important. This was article was about those Elite teams that had reduce their developer experience friction and mini mized the day to day toil from my first article. Now AI has accelerate that process. I believe this model is now more important than ever to invest in. 

## What does a developer produce?

While a developer does spend a significant portion of their day writing code, they are not trying to produce code, they are trying to produce software **–** working software that solves a customer problem. Code is a vital ingredient, yet it’s one element of a larger equation. 

Typically when companies look at optimizing productivity it starts with a reductive view of a developers day, a developer is endlessly coding, building and testing. While speeding up these tasks is incredibly important, we also need to look at the outcomes they are trying to achieve, to give us more insights into improving developer productivity. 

***![][image1]***

### Valuable

As 1,000 failed startups know, just because we built software, doesn’t mean anyone will use or pay for it. Finding ideas that are useful to customers, isn’t purely the job of the product manager or “the business”. Developers have an important contribution, and it is often overlooked. Some of the ways they contribute:

* Creating the high level requirements to achieve the desired outcome, in conjunction with product managers & design  
* Ideation, after going deep into the problem domain, developer will have a unique perspective  
* Designing an experiment to test an idea, with analytics instrumentation to get insights   
* Avoiding gold plating, finding simple ways to get the feature in front of customers to learn   
* Micro-decisions, designing the details of the functionality, with domain experts and peers

We should also ask if a user knows the capability even exists? And do they know how to use it? This to avoid “checklist development”, where we build features requested by managers, but the end users don’t actually need it. A lot of waste in software is through maintaining software that no one or has little use. 

### Releasable 

A customer should be able to utilize our software. While this seems obvious, a good question to ask is how much of your current software product is truly accessible by a customer? Often large swatches aren’t released. These unreleased features are akin to inventory in a store room with a limited shelf life. They provide no value, and there is only a finite period a customer is willing to pay for your product before turning to an alternative.

In order to keep code up to date, developers shape their work and configure the software so that it can be incrementally released and quickly put in the hands of end users safely (practicing [continuous delivery](https://continuousdelivery.com/)). They also instrument for customer behavior tracking, so that we can learn from the incremental change. It is work that is incredibly important, it may not result in many changes in lines of code, but is a huge factor in productive teams.

### Efficient

Making software efficient includes the operating costs, cloud services, supportability costs. Developers make large and small trade-offs decisions as they build that will affect its operational efficiency. 

Efficiency also applies to the amount of code we accumulate. Code is expensive for the company, code has to be maintained, supported and tested. Instead developers if possible use the wide range of building blocks open to them – cloud services, SaaS products, and open-source libraries. The services may originate from internal teams, leveraging already-built business functionality, data products, or technical capabilities. Considering this during software development, trading off against time to market, reduces engineering waste. 

### Evolvable

The developer is not just completing the feature they are working on, they are making it easy to modify and extend in the future, usually by someone else. Custom code can last for over 10 years. We’re all too familiar with technical debt being cited as the reason why a team can’t accelerate. Developers spend a lot of time designing software to be easy to understand, support, and modify. The act of refactoring, which often reduces the lines of code, facilities this. 

In order to create valuable and quality products, the developer spends a lot of time designing, not just the initial design work, the evolutionary design, the decisions they make day to day. When working on existing code a developer needs confidence their changes won’t disrupt functionality. Developers spend a lot of time building a safety net – testing, observability and resilience practices. Without this they will need to conduct extensive manual checks. This makes the application less brittle to change, and encourages developers to refactor for better evolvability, reducing the amount of code and future maintenance toil. 

### Reliable 

Our applications need to be able to adapt with the demands of the customer, now and in the future. Two of the most important ones are performance and availability. When introducing new functionality developers must ensure they haven’t haven’t added a scaling bottleneck or heightened risk of an outage. Whether it's a sudden surge in traffic due to a viral campaign, or the need of immediate patching in response to a known vulnerability, the software needs to easily handle such scenarios. The developer adds telemetry, we can learn quickly the cause of an issue and quickly fix it. 

These 5 elements are major qualities, common in every project. There are many other important qualities a developer should be concerned about, that we could write about e.g  accessibility, security and compliance. A pragmatic developer, can make tradeoffs across all of these elements. They all exist in a spectrum and are applied in different ways for stages of a product. For example in earlier stages we are more concerned with testing ideas, later stages we are more concerned with efficiency.  

You may be reading this, and thinking that is pretty obvious. I list am listing these out to show how far away software developer is from a factory model. A productive developer will find the best way to make an impact, sometimes it is heads down coding a complex feature quickly, another might collaborating with design colleagues on creating a simpler UI workflow, or pairing with less senior developers to bring them to speed. To increase productivity we need a culture that enables and rewards developers for making the biggest contribution to the impact of the software product. 

### Factory vs Studio Model 

A way to represent these two views (the outdated view and the modern one), is a Factory vs Studio model. In a factory model, like car manufacturing, we are building the same product over and over to a high quality from a detailed specification. A studio model, such as creating a film, is a group of creative people collaborating towards a product that delights the customer and generates value for our business.

To apply the models to software product teams, this is the major differences we see in approaches, from the perspective of the developer: 

| Factory Model | Studio Model  |
| :---: | :---: |
| Developers have little understanding of customer needs | Developers have deep understanding of customer personas, frustrations and motivations  |
| Developers have little grasp of the business domain and mission | Developers are experts in the domain of the product and understand the company goals  |
| Progress is tracked by strict roadmap of features  | Progress is tracked via value delivered to customers |
| Little quantification of product goals into metrics and indicators  | Product strategy has clear goals, with leading and lagging indicators |
| Long project, Few checkpoints for feedback with customers and stakeholders | Short milestones, regular feedback loops, the team pivots when value isn’t being produced.  |
| Cross functional interactions are handoffs  | Technologists (product, design, data & developers, etc) collaboration closely on design and build  |
| Progress metrics are focused on output (code & features.) | Balance of delivery, friction and outcome based metrics.  |

Essentially with the studio model the whole team, including developers, work together to iterate to improve quality and the value of the product. The Studio model acknowledges that software product development is hard, it is not linear trajectory, it’s messy, we have to iterate and experiment until we get it right. To give us the best chance of success we need to use all the insights, skills and creativity the team possesses. 

## Principles of the Studio Model 

### **Everyone in the studio is a technologist:** 

### **Customer Empathy:** *Developers have deep understanding of customer personas, frustrations and motivations* 

The factory model relies on product managers and business analysts to handle the interactions with the customer. The developer doesn’t need to concern themselves with the distractions of talking to a user of the product they are building, they should focus their time on what they are good at, *coding*. Features are provided to developers as requirement documents; there doesn’t need to be interaction with the analyst until the feature is done, and ready for approval. The reasons for why should build a feature are vague, at worst not included. 

In the studio model, we start with the principle that developers can and should build empathy for the customer, they should understand who the customer is, the different types of customers, what motivates them and what are their feedback and frustrations with the product. Understanding of the customer, they are empowered to make many of the product decisions themselves. Requirements no longer need to be lengthy documents detailing every aspect. 

#### How to implement?

To foster this understanding, user research should be easily accessible to Technologists, outlining customer issues and needs. Create a customer research knowledge base for each product, accessible to the Studio, this helps both technologists on the teams, and can also be context for an Agent when you are using it to refine ideas. 

Doing good non biased research is a specialized skill, but it is greatly improved with SME involved, having trainers researchers and product mangers work with developers, has the advantage of improving the research because of the SME involvement and improving the understanding. 

Reading research reports summary, creating opportunities for technologists to observe the customer using the produce the product, having access to recorded sessions, with key examples of types of uses cases being part of onboarding.

### **Requirements are hypothesis:** Developers are experts in the domain of the product and understand the company goals 

Building the wrong product—one that doesn’t provide value—is by far the biggest cause of wasted productivity. Long projects that follow rigid plans with minimal feedback often lead to features that don’t have the expected impact, or worse, aren’t even used. The team may have impressive delivery statistics and be following Agile practices, but if their energy is spent in the wrong ways, it’s all for nothing. To avoid this, the studio model fosters a culture of experimentation—where teams are encouraged to test new ideas, admit failure when things don’t work, and pivot quickly.

The factory model doesn’t work because, unlike car manufacturing, we don’t know exactly what customers will pay for or what to build. A common anti-pattern I see is teams treating their backlog of requirements as guaranteed value creators. It’s better to treat these requirements as hypotheses. Until users are actually using or paying for your service, the hypothesis remains unvalidated.

Loss aversion, a concept in behavioral psychology, makes people naturally risk-averse, especially when the potential reward is low and the risk involves significant loss. We have to combat this tendency to be naturally conversations. The best companies strike a balance by taking acceptable risks and encouraging innovation without being overly conservative.

#### How to implement?

One of the problems project planning tools, is that it uses a left to right model. Everything has to go from left to right. While that makes sense for development tasks, when I am using the same tooling to show ideas, that are being validated, it’s hard to throw away those ideas. 

I like to represent Ideas a funnel. Similar to a conversion as a funnel, where we are starting the series of ideas, but the expectation is that a lot of them won’t make it. In the funnel we show the validation steps for the teams they have to go through. 

Is this not the same a user story? It can be, but it depends on the implementation of the team. If they are good about making each user story an incremental piece of value. You can also implement ideas as a higher level concept that. I have annoyed a few project managers, by not letting not including story points until a user has actually used a feature, rather than done, or even that it is deployed (often features sit behind release toggles). 

Not every feature need to go through regious use testing and A/B tests. If users are complaining about a particulalr issue then we don’t need to do that, or if it’s something that can be included without drupting the flow, we still need to monitor the metrics for that feature, as an unused feature makes the code complex and has to be maintiend even if a few users are using it. 

### **Ideas come from anywhere:** Developers are experts in the domain of the product and understand the company goals 

The studio model counters this by maintaining a close feedback loop with customers. Teams challenge themselves to design experiments that test ideas in the leanest, quickest way possible to learn rapidly. Failure is celebrated as a learning opportunity, allowing teams to quickly discard unsuccessful experiments and move on to better ideas.

The key advantage here is the continuous delivery of value. By building incrementally with small batch sizes and short feedback loops, we can completely transform how we measure progress. When we have far away deliverables, 6 months, or even, a year long, it is too much to be able to reason about, so we have to resort to tracking progress with delivery metrics, we have little other information.  Small milestones allow the team to reason through changes, make trade-offs, and move away from hypothetical scenarios. With real data, decisions are based on facts, enabling the team to optimize for business outcomes

### **Optimize time to learning:** 

The focus on the entire Studio is to learn and iterate. Continous improvment is typically based on reducing technical debt, developer friction and improving the delivery model. We should still do this, the Studio Model does not work when the developer are bholen to technical debt and there is a long lead time. However in addition the key to the Sutdio model is challenging themselves, we can map out the process for learning, inclyding the validation steps. 

An anti-pattern, I have encouerted for companies that have large amount of users, is assuming everything has to be statically relevant infomraiont. Creating an A/B test can be expensive, if basically has to be production grade, as you have the chance.
